claim_text: Attackers broke into 24 Check Point management servers at 22 organisations
summary: GreyNoise says an attacker it calls GT13 controlled at least 24 Check Point Security Management Servers at 22 organisations, with activity it confirmed between Oct 17 and Nov 2, 2026.
detail: GreyNoise saw the intrusions from a relay server the attacker had taken over, where results and stolen data from the victims' Check Point servers were saved. BleepingComputer, SecurityWeek and Cybersecurity Dive all report it, but all rely on the GreyNoise report, so they count as one source. Check Point told BleepingComputer on Nov 25 that it is aware of the activity, but it did not confirm the count of servers or organisations, and no victim has spoken publicly.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: A named security firm's own investigation describes the intrusions; no victim, Check Point or government statement confirms them yet.
notes: Researcher report, Tier 3, relayed by three Tier 2 outlets. One independence group.

claim_text: A flaw in Check Point management servers (CVE-2026-16232) has been exploited by attackers
summary: Check Point said in July 2026 that this login bypass in its Security Management servers was being exploited in the wild against a handful of customers. CISA lists it as a known exploited flaw.
detail: Check Point's advisory says the attacks hit only management servers reachable from the internet with no limit on which computers may log in. It says all affected customers were notified. CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on July 22, 2026. GreyNoise says the GT13 attacker used this flaw on victims' servers in October.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: Check Point's own advisory and CISA's catalog both say the flaw was used in real attacks.
notes: Vendor admission plus CISA KEV, both Tier 1. This confirms the flaw was exploited (July); it does not on its own confirm the 22 GT13 victims.

claim_text: How the attacker first got into the Check Point servers
summary: GreyNoise says the attacker already had access to the Check Point servers before it saw them, and it could not tell when or how that access was gained.
detail: GreyNoise saw CVE-2026-16232 used after the servers were already compromised. Check Point told BleepingComputer on Nov 25 that the attackers used CVE-2026-16232, but it did not say whether that flaw was how they first got in. No source says how the first break-in happened.
label: Not established
why_it_supports: The researchers say they do not know, and no other source says.
notes: Root cause not published. s010, a Hacker News discussion, is cited only as where readers ask whether every victim exposed its console; it is not evidence.

claim_text: Check Point says the attackers used a known flaw that it disclosed in July
summary: Check Point told BleepingComputer on Nov 25 that it is aware of the activity GreyNoise describes and that the attackers used CVE-2026-16232, a flaw it disclosed in July 2026.
detail: Check Point's statement says: "This vulnerability and available protections are therefore not new," and that the attackers used an adaptation of the public Metasploit module for the flaw. It does not confirm GreyNoise's count of 24 servers at 22 organisations, name any victim, or say whether the flaw was the first way in. Until Nov 25 this claim said Check Point had not commented: BleepingComputer and Cybersecurity Dive had each asked and had no reply on Nov 24.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: BleepingComputer's Nov 25 update to its article quotes a Check Point spokesperson's statement in full.
notes: Check Point's own words, relayed by one outlet; no Check Point page carries it. Was 'Check Point has not commented on the GreyNoise report' until Nov 25.

claim_text: The attacker copied firewall databases, credentials and internal certificate files
summary: GreyNoise says the attacker launched over 100 management tasks on victims' Check Point servers, copying the firewall database and internal certificate authority, and stealing credentials and firewall settings.
detail: GreyNoise also says the attacker made a new certificate in one victim's network, switched off security policies there (which would disable the firewall), and tried to move into other systems such as Citrix, Ivanti, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange and domain controllers. A bulk task sent to all 24 servers on Oct 26 failed, GreyNoise says.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: The researchers describe what they saw the attacker do; no victim has confirmed it.

claim_text: Victims are in 17 countries and several industries, including the US
summary: GreyNoise says the victims have systems in 17 countries, including the US, UK, France, Germany, India, South Korea and Australia, in finance, energy, government, transport, mining, engineering and manufacturing.
detail: GreyNoise says the targeting did not seem to focus on any one country or industry. It has not named any victim.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: The researchers list the countries and sectors; no victim has come forward.

summary: No victim has been named by GreyNoise, Check Point, a government or any outlet we read.
detail: GreyNoise says it is working with international government partners and national computer emergency teams to notify victims. Do not guess names from outside commentary.
label: Not established
notes: Do not add names from social media or leak sites.

summary: GreyNoise does not tie GT13 to any known hacking group or country and says it cannot judge the attacker's motive.
detail: GreyNoise notes that the attacker was active during working hours in UTC+7 or UTC+8 and that one domain it used was first registered with a Vietnamese address, but it says it puts little weight on either. BleepingComputer says the activity resembled espionage but the motive could not be determined.
label: Not established
why_it_supports: The researchers say they cannot attribute it, and no government has.
notes: Attribution: none. Keep the time-zone hint out of the summary; GreyNoise itself discounts it.

claim_text: The attacker used AI tools to automate the attacks
summary: GreyNoise believes the attacker used AI language models and automated agents to scan, exploit, build tools and work the compromised servers, alongside hands-on human activity.
detail: This is GreyNoise's assessment from the automation and mistakes it saw. BleepingComputer notes the use of AI in this campaign remains unconfirmed.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: The researchers say they believe it; nobody else has checked it.

claim_text: The campaign is still going on
summary: GreyNoise lost sight of the attacker around Nov 2, 2026, but expects the campaign is ongoing because the attacker kept access to victims' Check Point servers.
detail: This is an expectation, not an observation. No source reports activity after Nov 2.
label: Unverified
why_it_supports: The researchers say they expect it; they say they could not see past Nov 2.
notes: Revisit on any CERT or Check Point notice.

claim_text: A separate attack wave hit Check Point firewalls (PHP2Shell), which GreyNoise says is unrelated
summary: Check Point said on Nov 12 that attackers exploited a PHP flaw (PHP2Shell) and a second bug in unpatched Check Point Security Gateways from Oct 30, compromising a couple of dozen systems in one region.
detail: That wave hit firewall gateways, not the management servers in the GreyNoise report, and in some cases included destructive activity, Check Point says. Cybersecurity Dive reports that GreyNoise confirmed the dates overlap but says the two campaigns are not related.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: Check Point's own advisory says its customers' gateways were compromised in that wave.
notes: Confirmed applies to the PHP2Shell wave itself (vendor admission, Tier 1). 'Not related' to GT13 is GreyNoise's word via Cybersecurity Dive only.

claim_text: Check Point released a fix in July 2026
summary: Check Point fixed CVE-2026-16232 in Jumbo Hotfix updates released July 22, 2026: R81.20 Take 158, R82 Take 118 and R82.10 Take 36 or later.
detail: Check Point also tells customers to allow management logins only from trusted addresses, put management behind a firewall, and search audit logs for 'application token' logins. It says Smart-1 Cloud customers are already protected. GreyNoise has published warning signs that defenders can check for.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: Check Point's own support article lists the fixed versions and steps.
